extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants, agents, and practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: examining patent utility and claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating asserted utility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (and related 35 U.S.C. 112 issues) during patent examination, and for construing claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification. Covers burdens of proof, prima facie case requirements, evidentiary requests, special rules for therapeutic/pharmacological utilities, and claim interpretation standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of applicant's statement of utility (Langer standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification disclosure which contains a teaching of the manner and process of making and using the invention . . . must be taken as in compliance with the enabling requirement of the first paragraph of § 112 unless there is reason to doubt the objective truth of the statements contained therein which must be relied on for enabling support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should presume that a statement of utility made by the applicant is true and should not begin by questioning its truth; instead they must first ask whether there is any reason to question the truth. If the asserted utility is credible (i.e., believable based on the record or the nature of the invention), a rejection based on lack of utility is not appropriate. (Cites In re Langer; In re Brana.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard: preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 is a question of fact and the evidentiary standard throughout ex parte examination in setting forth a rejection is a preponderance of the totality of the evidence under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overcome the presumption of truth, Office personnel must establish that it is more likely than not that one of ordinary skill in the art would doubt the applicant's statement of utility. Examiners must provide evidence sufficient to show the statement would be considered false by a person of ordinary skill, taking into account both facts and reasoning. (Cites Raytheon v. Roper; In re Oetiker; Herman v. Huddleston.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility test for an asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An assertion of utility is credible (believable to a person of ordinary skill in the art) unless (A) the logic underlying the assertion is seriously flawed, or (B) the facts upon which the assertion is based are inconsistent with the logic underlying the assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility refers to reliability based on the logic and facts offered by the applicant. 'Incredible utility' is a conclusion reached only after evaluating both the assertion and the evidentiary basis; examiners must not start with a presumption that an asserted utility is per se incredible or speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an asserted utility may be considered incredible
rubrics_metrics.description: An assertion may be not credible where a person of ordinary skill would consider the assertion 'incredible in view of contemporary knowledge' and nothing offered by the applicant counters what contemporary knowledge suggests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples sustaining 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections include assertions that violate scientific principles (e.g., second law of thermodynamics) or are wholly inconsistent with contemporary technical knowledge. Special care is required with therapeutic utilities: prior lack of success or absence of animal models alone should not typically defeat credibility. (Cites In re Gazave.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden: prima facie case and evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly reject a claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 101, the Office must (A) make a prima facie showing that the claimed invention lacks utility, and (B) provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in establishing the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must be well-reasoned and specific; examiners should provide documentary evidence when possible (journals, treatises, patents) or explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions if documentary evidence is unavailable. Mere questioning of operability is insufficient—factual reasons that would lead one skilled in the art to question the objective truth must be set forth. (Cites In re Gaubert; In re Oetiker; Fregeau v. Mossinghoff.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Required elements of a prima facie showing for lack of specific and substantial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted utility is not specific or substantial, the prima facie showing must establish that it is more likely than not that a person of ordinary skill would not consider any asserted utility to be specific and substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must contain: (A) an explanation that clearly sets forth the reasoning used in concluding the asserted utility is neither both specific and substantial nor well-established; (B) support for factual findings; and (C) an evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required elements of a prima facie showing for lack of credible specific and substantial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible, the prima facie showing must establish that it is more likely than not that a person skilled in the art would not consider credible any specific and substantial utility asserted by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must contain: (A) an explanation clearly setting forth the reasoning used in concluding the asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible; (B) support for factual findings relied upon; and (C) an evaluation of all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing when no specific and substantial utility is disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no specific and substantial utility is disclosed or well-established, a prima facie showing of no specific and substantial utility need only establish that applicant has not asserted a utility and that, on the record before the examiner, there is no known well-established utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must use specificity in setting forth initial rejections so applicants can identify and respond to assumptions made by the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity requirement in rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: It is imperative that Office personnel use specificity in setting forth an initial rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and support any factual conclusions made in the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity helps the applicant identify assumptions and properly address them. Examiners must explain factual bases and reasoning rather than make conclusory statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When examiners may request evidentiary support from applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: In appropriate situations the Office may require an applicant to substantiate an asserted utility for a claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for additional evidence should be imposed rarely, and only if necessary to support the scientific credibility of the asserted utility (e.g., assertion inconsistent with record and current scientific knowledge). When requesting evidence, the examiner should indicate why the record is defective and, where appropriate, what type of evidentiary showing can remedy the problem. Examiners must not demand redundant test data or unduly burden applicants. (Cites In re Pottier; In re Citron; In re Isaacs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shift and applicant's opportunities to rebut
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 has been properly imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may rebut by amendments to claims, arguments/reasoning, or new evidence (affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, or printed publications). New evidence must be relevant to the issues raised; conclusory declarations lacking nexus to supporting evidence have limited probative value. Examiners must fully consider and respond to each substantive element of any response; if the totality of the record makes the asserted utility more likely than not credible, the rejection cannot be maintained. (Cites In re Oetiker; In re Grunwell; In re Buchner; In re Rinehart.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of sufficiency and character of applicant's evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence that must be provided by an applicant to support an asserted utility; the required character and amount vary with what is claimed and whether the asserted utility contravenes established scientific principles or beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants need not prove utility beyond a reasonable doubt or with statistical certainty. Evidence is sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill to conclude the asserted utility is more likely than not true. Courts reversed 101 rejections where applicants supplied reasonable supporting evidence. (Cites Ex parte Ferguson; Nelson v. Bowler; Rey-Bellet v. Englehardt.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic/pharmacological utility: reasonable correlation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of pharmacological or other biological activity is relevant to an asserted therapeutic use if there is a reasonable correlation between the activity and the asserted utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable correlation can be shown by statistically relevant data, arguments/reasoning, documentary evidence (scientific articles), or combinations thereof. The applicant does not have to provide human clinical trial data; all that is required is reasonable predictiveness of the asserted use. (Cites Cross v. Iizuka; In re Jolles; Nelson v. Bowler.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity as supportive evidence for therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural similarity to a compound known to have a particular therapeutic utility can be supportive of an asserted therapeutic utility for a new compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should evaluate both the existence of the structural relationship and the applicant's reasoning explaining why the similarity is relevant. Structural similarity combined with evidence of substantial activity should be given appropriate weight. (Cites In re Jolles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro and animal testing as generally sufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Data generated using in vitro assays or from testing in an animal model, if reasonably correlated to the asserted therapeutic utility, generally will be sufficient to establish therapeutic or pharmacological utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must evaluate test parameters, choice of animal, relationship of activity to the disorder, characteristics of the compound, significance of data, and the applicant's explanation. Absence of an industry-accepted animal model is not dispositive; relevant animal tests with an appropriate explanation may be sufficient. (Cites Ex parte Maas; Ex parte Balzarini; In re Hartop; In re Krimmel.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Human clinical data not required to establish utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should not impose on applicants the unnecessary burden of providing evidence from human clinical trials to establish utility for inventions related to treatment of human disorders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no decisional law requiring human clinical trial data; courts have not required human data even where no art-recognized animal models exist. If an applicant has initiated human clinical trials, examiners should presume the subject matter of that trial is reasonably predictive of the asserted therapeutic utility. FDA review or approval is persuasive but not required; examiners must still be able to carry the burden of showing lack of sound rationale when experts (e.g., FDA) have found the rationale satisfactory. (Cites In re Isaacs; In re Langer; Ex parte Balzarini; In re Brana.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on requesting safety or efficacy data
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper for Office personnel to request evidence of safety in the treatment of humans or regarding the degree of effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should confine review to statutory patentability requirements and not impose requirements that belong to other agencies (e.g., FDA). Requests for human safety/efficacy data are outside the patentability inquiry. (Cites In re Sichert; In re Hartop; In re Anthony; In re Watson; In re Krimmel.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of claims directed to treatment of diseases with no prior cures
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to methods of treating or curing a disease for which there have been no previously successful treatments warrant careful review for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior lack of a cure is not a basis to conclude lack of utility. Examine the specification and evidence: claims to symptomatic treatments may require modest evidence; claims asserting a 'cure' may require significantly greater evidentiary support. Expert affidavit evidence with sound reasoning may suffice to establish credibility for use in previously untreatable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation: broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO construes claims based on claim language and the specification as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art, applying the broadest reasonable construction allowed to establish a clear record of what applicant intends to claim. This standard differs from claim interpretation in court proceedings, where claims are not given the broadest reasonable interpretation. (Cites Phillips v. AWH; In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr.; 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).)
